title: Mother's laundry work and being the sickly youngest boy
summary: His mother took in laundry and brought the children along; Ramey played on being the small, sickly baby boy.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Well, what did your mother do?

Well, my mother was more or less a housewife, but she also did laundry, like that. And she took us with her. And we used to be so ashamed, you know. She'd take the three boys and my baby sister, when she went to washing in those people's back yards. We had to go, too. And that was an effort to be sure we weren't into any trouble in the -- back home.
Well, were you any help to her, as you grew up?

Well, naturally my sister would -- usually they'd take her out and sit her down somewhere, and give her some toys to play with, or something. But one of my brothers was on that old big, black pot that you boil the clothes in. My mother was on the wash, and my other brother and I were on the two rinses, you know. I was on the pot next to my mother,
so that always gave her a chance where she could pop me, you know, when I didn't -- she'd never even raise -- wet hands with soap, and everything, would be right in my --
Well, where did you come in this quartet? Were you the youngest?

Yeah, I was the youngest boy, but older than my baby sister. And let me tell you, I used that, too. I really played that thing, took advantage of the fact that I was the baby boy. I used it on everybody I saw. We had to cut wood, you know --

Yeah, I was more or less a midget. I was kind of sickly. And I used that, too, you know. My mother would tell me, go out and bring in an armload of wood, and I'd grab my stomach. "My stomach feels bad," you know. If I didn't get the food I wanted, I had another alibi, you know. But it was wonderful living in Austin. Maybe later on I'll kind of expand on that.
